findings.headline: Strategic IT Development capital reduced by £1.5m (60%) with potential ongoing slippage
findings.detail: Chief Executive Directorate Strategic IT Development budgeted at £2.5m but forecast at £1m, a £1.5m variance. Council flags potential slippage with proposals to be confirmed during the year.
findings.matters: Strategic IT infrastructure delays can cascade through operations; uncertainty about digital transformation investment at Q1 signals resource or prioritisation constraints
findings.figures: Budget £2,500k, Forecast £1,000k, Variance (£1,500k)

findings.paper_title: Annex Fii - 2026-27 Cap Inv Prg - FO Summary and Detail - Qtr 1
findings.headline: HRA fire safety and building compliance capital slipped by £9m; only £2.9m of £11.9m Apartments/Compliance/Fire Safety budget forecast to be spent
findings.detail: Housing Revenue Account shows £13.6m underspend (20% variance). Largest single component is Apartments, Compliance & Fire Safety: budgeted £11.9m but forecast £2.9m only (£9m shortfall). Council attributes to design stage delays with plan of works to be reviewed in Q2. Decent Homes also £3.9m underspent.
findings.matters: Fire safety and regulatory compliance work on housing is safety-critical; delay of £9m in this area signals either governance issues or financial constraints in council housing maintenance, creating potential liability and regulatory risk
findings.figures: HRA total variance (£13,573k); Apartments/Compliance/Fire Safety budget £11,883k, forecast £2,914k, variance (£8,969k); Decent Homes budget £21,530k, forecast £17,631k, variance (£3,899k)
findings.quote: Homes England grant received in Quarter 1, plan of works to be reviewed and budgets potentially to be re-profiled during Quarter 2. Other slippages are due to delays in the design stages of some projects.

findings.detail: Supported Living - Step Up Step Down capital project budgeted at £4m has zero forecast outturn at Q1. No delivery is expected in 2026/27, with the council noting a review is underway and proposals to be confirmed.
findings.matters: Full deferral of planned adult social care capital signals either funding constraints or project delays affecting planned accommodation provision and service capacity
findings.figures: Budget £4,000k, Forecast £0k, Variance (£4,000k)
findings.quote: Review underway in relation to Supported Living - Step Up Step Down, forecast outturn will be monitored and updated each quarter.

findings.paper_title: Annex Fii - 2026-27 Cap Inv Prg - FO Summary and Detail - Qtr 1
findings.headline: Commercial Development capital project reduced by £16.5m (71%) with no confirmed scope or direction
findings.detail: Resources Directorate Commercial Development budget of £23m reduced to £6.5m forecast, a £16.5m variance at Q1. The council states a review is underway with proposals to be confirmed during the year and outturn monitored quarterly. This represents a material uncommitted reduction in planned investment with no stated recovery plan.
findings.matters: Commercial investment underspends with unconfirmed direction signal either delayed regeneration investment or scope reduction; this level of uncertainty on £16.5m is material for cash planning and lender risk assessment
findings.figures: Budget £23,000k, Forecast £6,500k, Variance (£16,500k)
findings.quote: Review underway in relation to Commercial Development, proposals to be confirmed during the year, forecast outturn will be monitored and updated each quarter.

findings.headline: Council has committed £10,000 for an external financial improvement adviser in 2026/27
findings.detail: The s151 Officer has approved funding for an external financial improvement adviser as a strategic contingency commitment in 2026/27. This was approved in consultation with the Cabinet Member for Finance.
findings.matters: An external improvement adviser appointment signals that the council's finance leadership recognizes areas where external expertise is required, which would be of concern to a lender assessing the council's financial management capability and capacity to manage debt.
findings.figures: £10,000 approved in 2026/27
findings.quote: External Financial Improvement Adviser  (10)

findings.headline: Council using capital receipts flexibility and reserves to offset revenue overspends; no Section 114 report yet, but mitigations are finite.
findings.detail: To manage social care overspends, the council has deployed £2m from corporate reserves earmarked for adult social care risks and £3.293m in capital receipts flexibility to support transformation. Section 151 Officer has not triggered a Section 114 report (which would indicate the council cannot meet spending commitments), noting ongoing mitigations are in place. However, using capital receipts for revenue and drawing reserves are one-time actions; they cannot be repeated indefinitely.
findings.matters: Capital receipts flexibility and reserve drawdown are tools of last resort. Their deployment signals the council is using contingency strategies to manage a £13.6m social care overspend. If overspends persist into Q2-Q4, these tools will be depleted.
findings.figures: £2m corporate reserve deployed; £3.293m capital receipts flexibility deployed
findings.quote: Despite the in-year pressures currently facing the Council, the Section 151 Officer has not considered it necessary to make any such report at the current juncture in light of ongoing mitigations.

findings.headline: DSG High Needs Block overspend of £19m; cumulative historic deficit £33.6m; government support covering only 90% of deficit conditional on reform.
findings.detail: High Needs Block forecasts £19m overspend in 2026/27 due to costs of Independent Specialist Providers and non-independent placements. DSG carries cumulative historic deficit of £33.6m as of 31 March 2026. Government's High Needs Stability Grant is expected to fund 90% of the historic deficit, conditional on full participation in national SEND reform during 2026. This means £3.36m of the cumulative deficit remains unfunded, and ongoing DSG support depends on reform success.
findings.matters: DSG deficit is structural, not cyclical. Even with government support, 10% of historic deficit (£3.36m) is unfunded. Current-year overspend will recur unless SEND reform reduces placement demand.
findings.figures: £19.0m current-year High Needs overspend; £33.6m cumulative deficit (31 March 2026); High Needs Stability Grant covers 90% of historic deficit
findings.quote: The DSG continues to carry a historic deficit with the cumulative deficit standing at £33.6 million as at 31 March 2026... The forecast position at the end of June 2026 is an overspend of £19.0 million relating in its entirety to the High Needs Block.

findings.headline: Adult Social Care overspend of £8.7m exceeds budget contingency even with £5.3m emergency adjustment; market capacity strain cited.
findings.detail: Adult Social Care forecast £8.7m overspend by Q1, attributed to demand challenges, health changes, and increased care package costs. Reduction in post-hospital funded nursing care eligibility and increased negative Continuing Healthcare assessments are driving market capacity strain and higher placement costs. The council has deployed £5.293m to partially offset this (£2m corporate reserve for adult social care risks, £3.293m capital receipts flexibility to support transformation). Section 3.10 notes 'the financial impact is higher than expected' despite budget provision.
findings.matters: Adult social care is the council's largest service cost and is demand-driven. Exceeding budget assumptions by 37% (£8.7m on a typical £23m+ budget) suggests demographic or eligibility changes the council did not model.
findings.figures: £8.7m overspend; £5.293m deployed mitigation (£2m reserve, £3.293m capital receipts flexibility)
findings.quote: Whilst care pressures were reflected in the budget for 2026/27, the financial impact is higher than expected. A reduction in the number of individuals assessed as eligible for funded nursing care following hospital discharge, alongside an increase in negative Continuing Healthcare assessments have contributed to ongoing capacity pressures within the care market and increased placement costs across the sector.

findings.headline: Children in residential care rising despite £4.9m overspend and active improvement plan; step-down strategy still being formulated.
findings.detail: Children's Services shows 1,058 children in care as of 22 June 2026, with residential admissions (highest-cost placement type) increasing in recent months. Despite a Children's Services Improvement and Delivery Plan with three stated imperatives—reducing demand, increasing foster care sufficiency, and developing relational practice—the service continues to overspend. Finance assurance meetings and step-down plans are being formulated, suggesting intervention is nascent rather than proven.
findings.matters: Residential placements are non-discretionary and high-cost. Rising numbers despite active improvement planning indicates demand pressures are outpacing mitigation speed.
findings.figures: 1,058 children in care (22 June 2026); £4.9m Q1 overspend
findings.quote: There were 1,058 children in care as at 22 June 2026, with the number of children admitted to residential care (the most expensive placement type) increasing over the last few months.

findings.headline: General Fund overspend of £6.7 million at Q1, with social care (Children's £4.9m + Adults' £8.7m) driving £13.6m of the pressure.
findings.detail: By end of June 2026, the council has identified £6.7m net overspend despite setting a balanced budget in February. Children's Services is £4.9m over due to rising numbers in residential care placements. Adult Social Care is £8.7m over, with the council offsetting this through £5.293m in budget virements (£2m from corporate reserve, £3.293m capital receipts flexibility). The overspend is not evenly distributed: social care accounts for £13.6m of pressure, offset only partially by underspends in other areas.
findings.matters: By month 3, the council is already off-budget by £6.7m, primarily in demand-led services that cannot be easily corrected. This suggests budget assumptions for social care demand were understated.
findings.figures: £6.7m net pressure; £4.9m Children's; £8.7m Adult Social Care; £5.293m mitigation (£2m reserve + £3.293m capital receipts)
findings.quote: As at the end of June 2026, a net pressure of £6.7 million has been identified primarily driven by high costs and demand in Children's and Adults' Social Care services.

findings.headline: Finance team capacity crisis: 7-month statutory reporting delay and material pension accounting errors
findings.detail: The council's finance team faced capacity pressures in 2024 while closing accounts for 2020/21 to 2022/23. The 2023/24 draft accounts were published in January 2025, seven months after the statutory May 2024 deadline. Audit procedures identified material errors in pension liabilities that required prior period adjustment, indicating quality review failures.
findings.matters: Finance team capacity issues directly undermine the reliability and timeliness of financial reporting. Material errors in a core liability (pensions £122m) that slip past internal controls suggest other misstatements may also exist undetected.
findings.figures: 7 months late on 2023/24 accounts (published January 2025 vs. May 2024 deadline); accounts backlog 2020/21–2022/23
findings.quote: The Council published its 2023/24 draft Statement of Accounts in January 2025, 7 months after the statutory deadline of May 2024... The work we did perform on the 2023/24 draft financial statements identified material errors relating to pension liabilities that also required a prior period adjustment.

findings.headline: Council unable to balance budget; received £21.7m exceptional financial support in 2024/25 with continued reliance into 2026/27
findings.detail: The auditor identified that 'As part of the 2024/25 budget setting, the Council made a request for, and received, £21.7m of Exceptional Financial Support from the Government as the Council could not meet its spending commitments from available resources.' The auditor classifies this as evidence of a significant weakness in financial sustainability. The council has continued to rely on EFS for 2025/26 and has included it in the 2026/27 budget.
findings.matters: A council unable to budget within available resources and requiring government bailouts to function demonstrates structural overspend. Continued reliance in three consecutive years with no exit plan indicates the underlying deficit is not being closed.
findings.figures: £21.7m Exceptional Financial Support 2024/25; continued reliance 2025/26 and 2026/27
findings.quote: As part of the 2024/25 budget setting, the Council made a request for, and received, £21.7m of Exceptional Financial Support from the Government as the Council could not meet its spending commitments from available resources. In our view, this is evidence of a significant weakness in arrangements that exposes the Council to significant financial risk.

findings.headline: Dedicated Schools Grant deficit of £22.4m; statutory protection expires March 2028
findings.detail: The council posted a DSG deficit of £22.4m in 2024/25. The Government's statutory override allowing councils to record DSG deficits outside useable reserves is extended only to March 2028. On expiry, the council must incorporate the cumulative deficit into useable reserves. At 31 March 2025, the General Fund balance was £14.8m plus £39.8m earmarked reserves — insufficient to absorb a £22.4m hit without severely constraining operations.
findings.matters: This is a imminent and material threat to reserves. In 16 months, the council loses statutory protection and must restate reserves downward by £22.4m, leaving it with minimal buffer and likely breaching borrowing covenants or prudency thresholds.
findings.figures: £22.4m DSG deficit at 31 March 2025; General Fund Balance £14.8m; earmarked reserves £39.8m; override expires March 2028
findings.quote: Stoke-on-Trent Council has posted a further DSG deficit for the year ended 31 March 2025, being £22.4 million as set out in the 2024/25 Statement of Accounts... On expiry of the override, the Council would need to incorporate the cumulative deficit in its useable reserves.

findings.headline: Third consecutive disclaimer of opinion; auditor unable to complete full audit procedures within statutory deadline
findings.detail: The council received disclaimed opinions on its 2022/23, 2023/24, and 2024/25 accounts. The auditor states the disclaimer was issued because 'there was not sufficient time to complete all required audit procedures in advance of the backstop date'. As a result, the auditor has no assurance over opening balances for the 2025/26 financial statements.
findings.matters: Three consecutive years without an audit opinion represents a severe break in accountability. No third-party audit verification of financial statements is highly material to creditors assessing the council's true financial position.
findings.quote: In March 2026, we disclaimed our opinion on the Council's 2024/25 financial statements. This followed on from disclaimed opinions issued previously in respect of the Council's. 2023/2024 accounts.

findings.headline: Full Council virement approval threshold raised from £500,000 to £2,000,000
findings.detail: The council is increasing the level at which Cabinet can approve budget movements without Full Council sign-off, from £500,000 to £2,000,000. This aligns practice with comparable authorities such as Southampton (£2,000,000) and Coventry (£1,500,000). The stated rationale is improved operational efficiency and faster decision-making, while retaining Full Council oversight of the largest budget movements.
findings.matters: Delegation of budget movement authority affects financial control and governance; a lender assesses whether the council's budget framework remains robust and proportionate to the scale of operations.
findings.figures: £500,000 (previous threshold), £2,000,000 (new threshold); Southampton £2,000,000, Coventry £1,500,000
findings.quote: The proposed amendment would increase the threshold for Full Council approval from £500,000 to £2,000,000, enabling Cabinet to approve virements up to that level.

findings.headline: Council continues to receive disclaimed audit opinions despite signing off 2024/25 accounts, with multi-year rebuild timeline ahead
findings.detail: The council has finalised its 2024/25 accounts after resolving team instability in the finance function, but continues to receive disclaimed audit opinions due to historic challenges. Management confirmed it expects it will take a number of years before achieving a fully completed audit. External auditors have reported exceptions on the council's arrangements for economy, efficiency and effectiveness in the use of resources.
findings.matters: Disclaimed audit opinions are a critical governance red flag for lenders assessing financial reliability and internal controls. A multi-year timeline to resolution indicates systemic issues requiring substantial remediation.
findings.figures: Multi-year timeline to clean audit; external audit opinion issued 25 March 2026
findings.quote: it continued to receive disclaimed audit opinions as a result of historic challenges. It was therefore anticipated that it might take a number of years before the Council was able to achieve a fully completed audit.

findings.paper_title: Internal Audit Annual Report 25-26 v2 (Proposed Final).docx
findings.headline: Overall audit opinion is Satisfactory but explicitly qualified by ongoing reviews
findings.detail: The Head of Audit and Fraud provides a 'Satisfactory' overall opinion on the control environment, but explicitly qualifies this as 'subject to the outcome of ongoing reviews'. Multiple significant audits are still in progress (Table 6) including Special Education Needs services where 'financial implications arising from EHCPs are appropriately controlled' is a specific audit objective.
findings.matters: A qualified audit opinion indicates material uncertainty about the true state of controls; the fact that financial control reviews for special needs are still pending suggests the final position on adequacy of controls is not yet confirmed
findings.figures: 34 reports issued with opinions; at least 6 significant audits in progress with opinions TBA
findings.quote: it has been concluded that the level of assurance on the adequacy and effectiveness of the City Council's control environment is "Satisfactory", subject to the outcome of ongoing reviews.

findings.paper_title: Internal Audit Annual Report 25-26 v2 (Proposed Final).docx
findings.headline: External delivery partnerships audit: no remediation progress by March 2026 deadline
findings.detail: An audit of Funding of External Delivery Partnerships and Programmes found control weaknesses in policy, procedures and monitoring, rated as 'Marginal'. Five recommendations were made, but as of 31 March 2026, none had been confirmed as implemented. The council committed to implementing all five by 30 June 2026.
findings.matters: This audit assesses whether the council's partnership investments are transparent and controlled; zero progress toward remediation three months after audit completion suggests governance control issues over significant external commitments
findings.figures: 5 recommendations (3 medium, 2 low); 0 implemented as of 31/03/26; deadline 30/06/26
findings.quote: Funding of External Delivery Partnerships and Programmes made five recommendations; three medium risks and two low risks, with the resultant audit opinion of "Marginal". The key areas which required improvement were in respect of policy, procedures and monitoring programmes and performance. The actions agreed to improve processes are all due to be implemented by the end of June 2026. As at the end of March 2026 none of the five recommendations had yet been confirmed as implemented.

findings.paper_title: Internal Audit Annual Report 25-26 v2 (Proposed Final).docx
findings.headline: Direct Payments service rated as Unsound with slow remediation
findings.detail: The Direct Payments audit (managing personal budgets for adults) received an 'Unsound' opinion due to fundamental governance and procedural weaknesses. The audit made 12 recommendations (5 high-risk, 7 medium-risk) covering governance framework, monitoring and administration. Only 3 of the 12 recommendations had been implemented by 31 March 2026.
findings.matters: Direct Payments controls a major personal budget allocation for vulnerable adults; fundamental control weakness here creates safeguarding and reputational risk, and slow implementation suggests difficulty in remediation
findings.figures: 12 recommendations (5 high, 7 medium); only 3 implemented as of 31/03/26
findings.quote: The Direct Payments audit made 12 recommendations; five high risks and seven medium risks, with the resultant audit opinion of "Unsound". The key areas which required improvement were in respect of the governance and procedural framework for the service, monitoring and admin istration. Actions were agreed to improve processes. At the end of March 202 6 internal audit were advised by management that three of the 12 recommendations had been implemented and work continued to address the remaining recommendations.

findings.headline: Adult Social Care also in overspend due to sustained demand and rising unit costs for placements
findings.detail: In addition to the £16.7m Children's Social Care overspend, the Adult Social Care directorate is also overspending 'due to sustained demand pressures, alongside rising unit costs for social care placements, particularly within residential and nursing care settings'. Specific drivers include reduction in Funded Nursing Care eligibility and unsuccessful Continuing Healthcare assessments pushing more demand to the council.
findings.matters: Two major social care services are both in overspend simultaneously, driven by demand and market cost inflation the council cannot control. This is a structural problem.
findings.figures: No specific overspend figure given for Adult Social Care; it is only described as 'overspend position'
findings.quote: the Adult Social Care and All Age Commissioning Directorate were also in an overspend position due to sustained demand pressures, alongside rising unit costs for social care placements, particularly within residential and nursing care settings

findings.headline: Section 151 Officer has not issued a Section 114 notice, but only conditionally and contingent on delivery of transformation
findings.detail: The Section 151 Officer (Chief Finance Officer) confirms they are not currently issuing a Section 114 notice (formal declaration of inability to balance the budget), but only 'contingent upon the successful delivery of the council's financial recovery, transformation and savings programmes'. The statement warns that failure to deliver transformation or secure continued EFS 'would significantly increase the council's financial risk and challenge its medium term financial resilience'.
findings.matters: A Section 114 notice is a legal declaration of financial failure. The fact the S151 is holding it back conditionally shows the council is on the edge. If transformation fails, this comes into play.
findings.figures: No specific figures; this is a binary risk
findings.quote: Whilst the Section 151 Officer is not currently minded to issue a Section 114 notice, this position remains contingent upon the successful delivery of the council's financial recovery, transformation and savings programmes and together with the continued effective management of emerging financial pressures. Failure to deliver the required pace of transformation, achieve planned reductions in demand led expenditure, secure ongoing support through the EFS framework where required, or realise the benefits of future funding reforms would significantly increase the council's financial risk

findings.headline: External auditor issued a disclaimer of opinion on the 2024/25 accounts, meaning no assurance is provided
findings.detail: The council's external auditor (Mazars) could not obtain sufficient audit evidence to form an opinion on the financial statements and issued a disclaimer. The council also missed the statutory deadline for publishing audited accounts (27 February 2026 deadline was not met). An action plan has been developed to strengthen financial reporting processes.
findings.matters: A disclaimer means the auditors could not verify the numbers are correct. This is a serious control weakness and makes it harder for anyone (lenders, government, the council itself) to trust the financial position.
findings.figures: Deadline: 27 February 2026; not met
findings.quote: the external auditor...would issue a disclaimer of opinion. A disclaimer indicates that the auditor was unable to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence to form an opinion and, therefore, no assurance is provided on the financial statements. The Accounts and Audit (Amendment) Regulations 2024 introduced a statutory backstop date requiring publication of audited local authority accounts for 2024/25 by 27 February 2026. This deadline was not met.

findings.headline: Exceptional Financial Support of £16.8m is temporary government life-support that reduces future flexibility
findings.detail: The council received government EFS in both 2024/25 and 2025/26 totalling £16.8m (£11m for Children's Social Care, £3m for transformation, £2.8m for interest costs). The governance statement explicitly states this 'reduces financial flexibility in future years and cannot be viewed as a sustainable long-term solution to the underlying financial challenges'.
findings.matters: EFS is not a permanent funding solution. The council is masking structural deficits with temporary government grants. When EFS ends, the underlying £16.7m Children's Social Care overspend and demand pressures will resurface.
findings.figures: £16.8m EFS accessed; £11m allocated to Children's Social Care, £3m to transformation, £2.8m to interest costs
findings.quote: Whilst this support has enabled the council to manage immediate financial pressures, it also reduces financial flexibility in future years and cannot be viewed as a sustainable long-term solution to the underlying financial challenges

findings.headline: DSG (Dedicated Schools Grant) accumulated deficit of £22.4m with statutory override ending in 2028
findings.detail: The council has accumulated a £22.4m deficit in the ring-fenced schools budget. External audit flagged this as a significant weakness. Critically, the statutory override that allows councils to carry forward DSG deficits ends in March 2028, meaning the council will need to find this money from its own budget or from the schools budget thereafter.
findings.matters: This is a time-bomb. The council cannot carry this deficit indefinitely. In 2028, either the council absorbs this from its general fund, or schools must cut spending. This creates a major financial cliff.
findings.figures: £22.4m DSG deficit as at 31 March 2025; statutory override ceases March 2028
findings.quote: the external auditor identified a significant weakness in the council's financial sustainability arrangements relating to the Dedicated Schools Grant (DSG) deficit, reported at £22.4m as at 31 March 2025. Recommendations include strengthening medium-term financial planning ahead of the cessation of the statutory override in March 2028

findings.headline: Children's Social Care overspend of £16.7m, indicating demand and placement costs are structurally unmanageable
findings.detail: The Children and Families Directorate spent £16.7m over budget in 2025/26 due to sustained demand and placement costs. This is part of a wider pattern where both Children's and Adult Social Care are described as creating 'a level of expenditure that remains financially unsustainable without further transformation and intervention'.
findings.matters: A £16.7m overspend in one service area is material. Combined with similar pressures in Adult Social Care, it shows the council's budget is broken and dependent on one-off mitigations and government support.
findings.figures: £16.7 million overspend in Children and Families Directorate
findings.quote: Children and Families Directorate overspent by £16.7 million largely due to the continued demand and placement costs relating to Children's Social Care

findings.headline: The council delivered only 73% of planned savings (£0.8m of £1.1m), with ongoing delivery failures expected
findings.detail: Of £1.1m in identified 2025/26 savings, only £0.8m were achieved as planned. The £0.3m shortfall required mitigating actions. The paper notes that unachieved savings 'will be monitored closely in the coming year', implying some may not materialise, further weakening the budget control environment.
findings.matters: Failure to deliver planned savings indicates weak budget management and suggests further unplanned pressures may emerge, given the council is already dependent on government bailout.
findings.figures: £1.1 million savings identified; £0.8 million delivered; £0.3 million shortfall
findings.quote: a total of £1.1 million savings were identified within the budget. As at the end of March 2026, £0.8 million of these saving proposals have been delivered as planned, while £0.3 million of these saving proposals were not achieved as originally proposed.

findings.headline: The 2026/27 budget also requires £10.5m in Exceptional Financial Support, with further gaps projected beyond that date
findings.detail: The council has already secured in-principle government agreement for £10.5m EFS for the next financial year. The paper indicates further requests will be considered for 2028/29 onwards, particularly in the context of potential Local Government Reorganisation, suggesting no clear exit from dependence on emergency support.
findings.matters: The council cannot currently project a sustainable financial position without continuing government bailout, with no visibility on when or if dependency will end.
findings.figures: £10.5 million EFS for 2026/27; original budget gap £31.2 million before management actions
findings.quote: The City Council submitted a further request to government for Exceptional Financial Support (EFS) for 2026/27 to address the remaining budget gap. An in principle agreement was subsequently received for £10.5 million of EFS support for 2026/27, which was incorporated into the City Council's approved Medium Term Financial Strategy (MTFS).

findings.headline: Over 15 years, the council's inflation-adjusted spending power has fallen 25% whilst demand for social care has risen substantially
findings.detail: This structural mismatch between declining resources and rising demand explains why the council cannot solve its financial challenges through management action alone. The paper notes that even the government's new Fair Funding Review settlement offers only average support, not sufficient to address this underlying disparity.
findings.matters: Lenders need to understand that this is not a cyclical budget problem but a structural mismatch that deteriorates annually, with limited options for resolution at local level.
findings.figures: 25% real-terms reduction in spending power over 15 years; sustained increases in demand for essential services
findings.quote: Over the past 15 years, Stoke-on-Trent City Council has experienced a real-terms reduction in spending power of around 25%, alongside sustained increases in demand for essential services.

findings.headline: The DSG (schools funding) deficit has reached £33.6m and will impact general council reserves when the statutory override expires in March 2028
findings.detail: The cumulative deficit grew from £22.4m at March 2025 to £33.6m by March 2026, an in-year increase of £11.2m. The statutory override currently quarantines this from the general fund, but when it expires in 2028, any remaining shortfall will be charged to council reserves. The council is relying on a High Needs Stability Grant (expected Autumn 2026) to cover 90% of the historic deficit.
findings.matters: A £33.6m latent liability will hit general reserves in two years unless the expected government grant arrives on schedule, creating a material threat to financial sustainability.
findings.figures: £33.6 million cumulative DSG deficit; £22.4 million at March 2025; £11.2 million in-year increase
findings.quote: any remaining deficit following national support measures would place significant pressure on usable reserves and wider council budgets.

findings.headline: Adult Social Care overspent by £14.6m due to demand growth and rising unit costs, with underlying position worse than budgeted and further pressure expected in 2026/27
findings.detail: The directorate faced significant demand pressures across all care types (residential, nursing, domiciliary, supported living). The actual outturn was worse than forecast because higher-acuity cases shifted from NHS Continuing Health Care to council funding. The paper notes that whilst some recurrent pressure was factored into 2026/27, there will be further unresolved pressure to manage.
findings.matters: Adult social care pressures are structural, driven by demographic and NHS access changes beyond council control, and show no sign of stabilising despite budget provisions.
findings.figures: £14.6 million overspend; pressures across residential, nursing, domiciliary and supported living services
findings.quote: the outturn position for 2025/26 in terms of underlying expenditure on personal care services is worse than projected at the time the budget was set. This was particularly the case in adult services, in part because of having to deal with more cases of higher acuity, as the NHS tightened access to Continuing Health Care and Funded Nursing Care.

findings.headline: Children's Services overspent by £16.7m, almost entirely driven by placement costs, with ongoing pressure on complex cases
findings.detail: Placement costs grew to £16.2m, increasing by £1m in the final quarter alone. The council held 1,071 children in care at year-end, with the paper noting that whilst overall numbers fell slightly, the number in expensive external residential settings remains high due to case complexity and insufficient foster care capacity. The Children's Improvement Plan has not yet resolved this pressure.
findings.matters: This is a recurring, structural overspend driven by uncontrolled demand that cannot be quickly reduced, indicating ongoing budget risk and limited service recovery options.
findings.figures: £16.7 million directorate overspend; £16.2 million placement overspend; 1,071 children in care
findings.quote: The forecast pressure relating to children's placements increased from £15.2 million at the end of Quarter 3 to £16.2 million at 31 March 2026, representing an increase of £1.0m, and explaining almost all the overspend position.

findings.headline: The council required £16.8m in Exceptional Financial Support to balance 2025/26, masking an underlying overspend of the same amount
findings.detail: Without government bailout, the council's net position would have been a £16.8 million overspend. The council also allocated £2.3 million to the Strategic Risk Reserve and deployed £5.5 million of capital receipts to support transformation costs. This indicates the underlying budget position is structurally unsustainable.
findings.matters: Dependency on government emergency funding to balance budgets signals severe structural financial fragility and creates uncertainty about repayment and future financial sustainability.

findings.detail: The council has increased the General Reserve to 5% of net revenue expenditure, which is the minimum recommended level, but acknowledges the ideal level would be 10%. The S151 officer states this higher level is 'not realistic at this point' due to current financial challenges. The CIPFA Financial Resilience Index (based on 2024-25 data) continues to show the council at high risk relative to peer authorities on reserve levels, indicating minimal buffer to absorb demand shocks or service pressures in social care.

findings.headline: Council borrowing £10.5m Exceptional Financial Support for 2026-27 that S151 officer states 'is not a sustainable or long-term solution'
findings.detail: Stoke-on-Trent is accessing Exceptional Financial Support, a temporary mechanism permitting councils to use capital resources to fund revenue spending. The council has requested £10.5m for 2026-27 and £7.5m for 2027-28. The S151 officer explicitly states this 'is not a sustainable or long-term solution to the council's underlying financial challenges and reliance on Exceptional Financial Support must be reduced and removed.' The council has cumulatively borrowed £69.5m through EFS since 2023-24, creating future year revenue liabilities through MRP and interest totaling £6.8m over four years.
findings.matters: Every year of EFS increases debt stock and future revenue commitments; the council's plan to repay through capital receipts is constrained by low land values and contamination from the city's industrial past

findings.quote: Whilst the receipt of Exceptional Financial Support enables the council to address its financial position in the short term and to set a balanced budget for the forthcoming financial year it is not a sustainable or long-term solution to the council's underlying financial challenges and reliance on Exceptional Financial Support must be reduced and removed over the MTFS period.

findings.headline: 2025-26 forecast overspend of £6.3m in Children's Services; council forced into 'very expensive individual placements' for complex young people
findings.detail: The council is forecasting a current-year overspend of £6.3m, primarily in Children and Family Services. As of December 2025, there are 1,095 children in care with a high proportion in expensive external residential placements. The document notes the council 'has had to make some very expensive individual placements for young people of very high complexity that each have a significant financial impact.' Any unmitigated overspend will be charged to reserves, which are already at minimum recommended levels. This is a live risk to the 2026-27 balanced position.
findings.matters: This demonstrates the council cannot reliably control demand-led service costs; continued uncontrolled growth would deplete reserves and undermine the ability to set balanced budgets in future years
findings.figures: 2025-26 forecast overspend: £6.3m, children in care (December 2025): 1,095, number in external residential placements described as high and above forecast
findings.quote: The council has had to make some very expensive individual placements for young people of very high complexity that each have a significant financial impact.

findings.headline: Council faces budget gaps of £16.3m (2027-28) and £23.7m (2029-30); S151 officer states 'this position cannot be mitigated by inaction'
findings.detail: Once Exceptional Financial Support and short-term flexibility measures are exhausted, the council faces structural budget gaps that can only be closed through a 'continuous programme of transformation' focused on contracts, agency reduction, children in care placements, digital transformation, and asset disposals. The S151 officer emphasizes the need for 'immediate and sustained work' to address these gaps and explicitly rejects the assumption that a future Local Government Review will resolve the underlying financial challenges.
findings.matters: Large and growing structural gaps indicate the council's income does not cover committed spend; failure to deliver transformation savings would force the council to request additional EFS, deploy reserves, or face insolvency
findings.quote: The council faces a significant financial gap in 2027-28 and beyond. This position cannot be mitigated by inaction, nor by any assumption that the future Local Government Review (LGR) will resolve the council's underlying financial challenges.

findings.headline: DSG High Needs deficit is 'serious and significant' risk; S151 officer would consider Section 114 notice if this remains unfunded beyond 2028
findings.detail: The council faces a growing deficit in special educational needs funding now held outside the General Fund under a statutory override expiring 31 March 2028. The deficit is growing from £22.4m (April 2025) to £36.1m (March 2026), forecast to reach £184.0m by March 2031 if current trends continue. The S151 officer explicitly states they would need to consider issuing a Section 114 notice if government funding does not continue after the override ends. The council is dependent on a High Needs Stability Grant and further national SEND announcements expected in 2026.
findings.matters: When the statutory override ends on 31 March 2028, this will become a live liability on the General Fund balance sheet unless national support is secured; without it, the S151 officer would be forced to issue a Section 114 notice
findings.figures: Opening April 2025: £22.4m, projected March 2026: £36.1m, forecast March 2031: £184.0m without further intervention
findings.quote: The Dedicated Schools Grant High Needs deficit presents a serious and significant financial risk to the council. In the absence of the statutory override, the Section 151 Officer would need to consider whether the council's financial position required the issuing of a Section 114 notice should funding and deficit pressures remain unaddressed.

findings.headline: S151 officer's opinion is conditional: will not issue Section 114 notice now only if required actions are taken and all assumptions are delivered
findings.detail: The Section 151 Officer states the budget is 'sufficiently robust' but explicitly conditions this on a series of actions being taken and MTFS assumptions being delivered. The document then warns that if these are not met, 'very serious consideration would need to be given to the issuing of a s114 notice in the future.' This is the formal insolvency mechanism for English councils, triggering government takeover and ceasing all non-essential spending.
findings.matters: A Section 114 notice would hand financial control to the government, freeze discretionary spending, and severely restrict the council's ability to borrow or invest
findings.figures: Conditional on delivery of actions across savings, DSG management, reserve building, and transformation programmes; no specific triggers quantified
findings.quote: Based on the above the s151 officer is not minded to issue a s114 notice at this point. This is predicated on the basis that the above actions are implemented in full and within the required timescales.

findings.detail: The council is conducting comprehensive condition surveys of its property portfolio in early 2026-27. These surveys will form the critical evidence base for the 25-year capital strategy and Asset Management Plan. The strategy currently has only indicative figures and will be refined once survey results are known, suggesting true asset condition is not yet understood.
findings.matters: Unknown asset condition creates risk of significant unplanned capital expenditure emerging once surveys complete. The £1.28bn budgeted for existing asset lifecycle works may prove insufficient.
findings.figures: 25-year pipeline includes ~£1.28bn for existing assets; survey results pending early 2026-27
findings.quote: A key next step is the completion of extensive condition surveys of the council's corporate estate which are due to take place in early 2026-27. These surveys will form a critical evidence base for the strategy, providing detailed lifecycle requirements and informing the council's Asset Management Plan.

findings.headline: A major decision on replacing the Hanford Waste-to-Energy plant is pending, with significant and unquantified capital and revenue implications
findings.detail: The document identifies replacement of the Hanford Waste-to-Energy plant—the facility responsible for processing the city's waste—as a major capital scheme requiring significant decisions. The 25-year strategy will need to set out the associated capital and revenue implications, but these are not yet quantified in this strategy.
findings.matters: Replacement of critical waste infrastructure is mandatory and typically very costly. Unknown costs and timing create planning uncertainty and could significantly strain the council's finances.

findings.headline: The council will need to borrow £303 million over the next three years, creating significant interest rate and refinancing risk
findings.detail: The funding strategy relies heavily on gap funding through borrowing. Over the 10-year capital programme (2026/27-2035/36), borrowing totals £351.162m. The first three years alone require £303m in new loans (2026/27: £112m, 2027/28: £61m, 2028/29: £46m). By 2036, the gap between existing loans and the liability benchmark reaches £632m.
findings.matters: Large borrowing requirements expose the council to interest rate volatility and refinancing risk, with significant unbudgeted costs possible if rates rise. This constrains financial flexibility.

findings.detail: The council explicitly states reserves are at minimum levels. Unearmarked General Fund reserves are forecast at 4.8% of net revenue expenditure as at 1 April 2026, below the 5% national benchmark recommendation. The council proposes only a £0.5m annual contribution to improve this.
findings.matters: Minimal reserves severely constrain financial resilience and the council's ability to absorb unexpected costs, emergencies, or revenue shortfalls, increasing default risk.

The council states explicitly that this reflects 'limited longer-term investment opportunities identified in the Authority's cash flow', suggesting the council lacks the cash surplus to commit funds beyond immediate needs.

If the council cannot spare cash to invest beyond one month, it has little buffer to absorb unexpected costs, capital accelerations, or revenue shortfalls—a concern for lenders assessing financial flexibility.

The forecast assumes £473m of gross capital programme borrowing and £132m of existing internal borrowing to be realised, creating a borrowing requirement of £547.7m over the decade.
findings.matters: A lender evaluates the sustainability of rising debt by comparing it to revenue growth and economic prospects. When debt is rising alongside above-average financing costs and constrained cash flow, the risk of future affordability stress increases.
findings.figures: £941.4m forecast end-2025/26; £1,021.7m by 2033/34; gross borrowing requirement £547.7m
findings.quote: the total expected gross borrowing over the next 10 years, taking account of points (i and ii) above, is estimated at £547.7m, of which £316.4m is general fund and £231.1m is HRA

findings.headline: New borrowing locks in rates 1 percentage point above the existing portfolio
findings.detail: The council borrowed £95m in the first three quarters at an average rate of 4.86%, raising the overall debt portfolio average from 3.80% to 3.85%. The previous opening rate was 3.75%; this is the highest rate at which the council has borrowed in recent years. Future debt service costs will be higher as a result.
findings.matters: Rising borrowing costs directly increase the council's future revenue commitments. Combined with already above-average financing ratios, higher rates on new debt reduce the council's budget headroom and increase the risk that future financial stress will force spending cuts or service reductions.
findings.figures: £95m borrowed at 4.86% average; overall portfolio now 3.85%
findings.quote: The City Council borrowed £95m PWLB EIP loans, for between 8 and 12 years at an average rate of 4.86%

findings.headline: Debt servicing costs are 66% above the peer group average
findings.detail: The ratio of financing costs to net revenue stream is 13.25% for 2025/26, compared to an average of 7.99% among 39 statistical neighbours. Stoke ranks 7th from highest in this metric. This means a larger share of the council's income is locked into debt service, constraining capacity for service investment or financial resilience.
findings.matters: A lender assesses debt affordability partly through this ratio. When it significantly exceeds peer averages, it signals that the council has less financial flexibility than comparable authorities and faces higher risk if revenues decline or costs rise unexpectedly.
findings.figures: 13.25% (Stoke) vs 7.99% (average); ranked 7th out of 39 councils
findings.quote: Stoke 13.25 Rank 7th [out of 39]... Average 7.99

findings.headline: Council's interest rate exposure exceeds its prudential indicator limit
findings.detail: The actual one-year revenue impact of a 1% interest rate rise is £503,148, exceeding the approved prudential limit of £408,000. This represents an unplanned exposure of approximately £95,000 to interest rate volatility beyond what the council's risk framework permits. The breach affects both upside and downside scenarios symmetrically.
findings.matters: A lender needs confidence that a council manages treasury risks within approved boundaries. A breach—whether from underestimated exposures or deliberate overshoot—indicates either that the council's risk assessment was flawed or that it has accepted uncontrolled risk, both of which reduce creditworthiness.
findings.figures: £408,000 limit; £503,148 actual exposure
findings.quote: Upper limit on one-year revenue impact of a 1% rise in interest rates £408,000... Actual £503,148

findings.headline: Statutory financial reporting significant weakness not yet fully addressed; 2024/25 statements included material errors requiring prior-period adjustment
findings.detail: The 2023/24 accounts, backstopped in December 2024, contained material errors requiring prior-period adjustments. The 2024/25 financial statements were not authorised for issue until 30 June 2025, seven months late. The auditors note the finance team faces capacity challenges and state they 'do not currently have sufficient evidence to confirm that the significant weakness has been fully addressed in 2024/25'.
findings.matters: Unreliable financial reporting with material misstatements, combined with late delivery, raises questions about the quality of management information on which the council relies. Lenders depend on timely, accurate accounts; serial failures erode confidence in management's oversight.
findings.figures: 2023/24 accounts backstopped 12 Dec 24 with material errors; 2024/25 accounts authorised 30 June 2025 (7 months late vs May 2024 deadline)
findings.quote: Whilst progress is being made, we do not current have sufficient evidence to confirm that the significant weakness has been fully addressed in 2024/25 as we have not performed sufficient testing over the 2024/25 financial statements to conclude all matters have been addressed.

findings.headline: General Fund reserves showing pattern of erosion; statutory override on DSG expires 2028 with £38.8 million cumulative deficit at risk to reserves
findings.detail: The council's General Fund Balance is £14.8m with earmarked reserves of £39.8m. The auditors observe an 'ongoing pattern of erosion' in reserves. By March 2028, the DSG statutory override expires. If the cumulative DSG deficit reaches the forecast £38.8m and the override ceases, the council would be forced to absorb this into useable reserves, materially depleting them.
findings.matters: Depleting reserves combined with persistent structural deficits leave the council with limited financial flexibility. Once the DSG override expires, a £38m charge to reserves would consume most liquid balances, severely constraining the council's ability to manage unexpected pressure or fund transformation.
findings.figures: General Fund Balance £14.8m; earmarked general fund reserves £39.8m; forecast cumulative DSG deficit at March 2026: £38.8m
findings.quote: We also examined the Council's General Fund reserves as presented in the financial statements, which shows an ongoing pattern of erosion, although whether this continues beyond 2026/27 will be, in part, influenced by the outcome of the fair funding review.

findings.headline: Children and Families Directorate forecast overspend of £9.5 million in 2025/26, largely driven by children in care rising to 1,085 against budget of 986
findings.detail: As of June 2025 (Q1 2025/26), the council had 1,085 children in care compared to a budgeted average of 986. This drove a £9.5m forecast overspend for the directorate, with £7.9m attributable to children's placements. Despite the council's May 2025 Ofsted rating of 'requires improvement', numbers and costs continue to exceed budget. Controls include restrictions on recruitment and non-essential spend, but these have not arrested the underlying pressure.
findings.matters: Rising demand for children's social care placements, combined with persistent inability to budget accurately for this service, creates a rolling pressure on reserves. The council has already drawn down general reserves and the trend shows no improvement even after two years of statutory direction and improvement activity.
findings.figures: 1,085 children in care as of 16 June 2025 vs budget of 986; £9.5m forecast overspend in Children & Families; £7.9m placement-related; Children in care March 2024: 1,156; end Q4 2024/25: 1,056
findings.quote: The number of children in care was 1,085 as of 16 June 2025, compared to a budgeted average of 986 and that increased reliance on independent residential placements has been a major contributor to this financial strain.

findings.headline: Continued reliance on Exceptional Financial Support despite general fund overspend of £21.4 million in 2024/25
findings.detail: The council's general fund overspent by £21.4m in 2024/25, covered entirely by EFS. For 2025/26, EFS of £16.8m has been agreed in principle. The auditors identify this as a 'significant weakness' in financial sustainability, with the council unable to close its budget gap through savings or income.
findings.matters: Repeated reliance on exceptional support (granted only when councils face genuine hardship) signals inability to balance operations. This weakens the council's borrowing capacity and indicates structural, not temporary, financial problems.
findings.figures: 2024/25 general fund overspend £21.4m; 2025/26 EFS £16.8m agreed in principle; 2025/26 forecast financial risks £13.7m
findings.quote: The ongoing reliance on EFS means there is a continued significant weakness in relation to financial sustainability.

findings.headline: Audit opinion disclaimed for the fourth consecutive year; 2024/25 disclaimer anticipated by February 2026
findings.detail: The council has received disclaimed audit opinions continuously since 2020/21 (2020/21, 2021/22, 2022/23, 2023/24). The auditors report that as of November 2025, rebuilding assurance work had not yet commenced, and there is insufficient time to complete audit procedures before the backstop deadline of 27 February 2026, making another disclaimer inevitable.
findings.matters: Four successive disclaimed opinions indicate persistent inability to produce auditable accounts. This signals serious control environment weakness and makes the council's reported figures unreliable for lending or treasury decisions.
findings.figures: Disclaimed opinions: 2020/21 (12 Dec 24), 2021/22 (13 Dec 24), 2022/23 (13 Dec 24), 2023/24 (27 Feb 25); anticipate 2024/25 disclaimer no later than February 2026
findings.quote: In October 2025, we provided the Audit & Standards Committee with an outline plan for rebuilding assurance, but as at November 2025, our work has not commenced, but our expectation is that there is insufficient time to complete sufficient audit procedures before the backstop date of 27 February 2026 and therefore a disclaimed opinion is anticipated no later than February 2026.

findings.headline: Cumulative Dedicated Schools Grant deficit of £22.4 million growing to forecast £38.8 million by March 2026
findings.detail: The council's DSG deficit increased by £10.0m in 2024/25 due to High Needs Block spend of £57.3m against funding of £46.5m. The auditors forecast a further £16.4m pressure in 2025/26. A government statutory override allowing DSG deficits to be excluded from reserves expires in March 2028, at which point the cumulative deficit would impact useable reserves directly.
findings.matters: An unresolved DSG deficit of this scale, combined with expiring statutory protection, creates material financial risk. If the override expires while the deficit remains, it forces either service cuts or further exceptional support from government.
findings.figures: £22.4m cumulative DSG deficit; £10.0m in-year deficit 2024/25; £16.4m forecast pressure 2025/26; High Needs Block spend £57.3m vs funding £46.5m
findings.quote: Stoke-on-Trent Council has posted a further DSG deficit for the year ended 31 March 2025, being £22.4 million...The Government's statutory override for DSG deficits, originally due to expire in March 2026, has been extended for a further two years to March 2028.

findings.headline: Disclaimed audit opinion due to government-imposed backstop date preventing completion of audit procedures
findings.detail: Stoke-on-Trent received a disclaimed audit opinion from external auditors for 2024/25 because the government's backstop date of 27 February 2026 restricted the time available for auditors to complete all required procedures. A disclaimed opinion means auditors were unable to obtain sufficient audit evidence to form a view on whether the financial statements give a true and fair view.
findings.matters: A disclaimed audit opinion indicates unresolved audit risk and incomplete verification of the council's financial position, which creates uncertainty for lenders about the reliability of reported figures.
findings.figures: Backstop date: 27 February 2026; Financial year: 2024/25
findings.quote: The City Council is has received a disclaimed audit opinion from the City Council's external auditors on the financial position of the Council for 2024/25 due to the backstop date issued by government restricting the time available for the auditors to complete all the required procedures in order to facilitate an opinion on the statement of accounts for 2024/25.

findings.headline: General Fund capital spending is heavily front-loaded at £183.8m in 2026/27, then drops 66% to £60.4m in 2027/28
findings.detail: The General Fund capital programme shows a sharp cliff profile, with spending of £183.8m required in year one, falling to £60.4m in year two and £8–9m annually from 2031/32 onwards. This pattern concentrates borrowing and cash-flow pressure into the immediate period and may reflect project completion deadlines or asset purchase windows.
findings.matters: Front-loaded capital spending increases immediate borrowing requirement and cash-flow pressure; a cliff in spending could indicate project slippage risk or completion pressure.

findings.headline: Section 151 Officer's assurance of meeting borrowing requirements is explicitly qualified by reference to 'the challenging financial environment'
findings.detail: The 151 Officer confirms no difficulty meeting debt requirements in 2025/26 or future years, but this assurance is conditional on the council's ability to manage a stated challenging financial environment. The document does not elaborate on this environment within this annex, but the qualification signals known headwinds to council finances.
findings.matters: A qualified statement from the 151 Officer indicates underlying financial stress and suggests the prudential indicators alone do not capture full financial risk.
findings.figures: No specific figures provided in this annex for the challenging environment
findings.quote: This view takes into account current commitments, existing plans and the proposals in the approved budget, but is subject to the challenging financial environment set out in this report.

findings.headline: Council's borrowing requirement rises from £931.9m to £1,045.2m over the decade, an increase of £113.3m or 12%
findings.detail: The borrowing element of external debt (excluding long-term liabilities) shows a steady upward trajectory across all ten years of the planning period. This reflects cumulative impact of approved capital programmes in both General Fund (£383.4m) and HRA (£475.2m).
findings.matters: Rising debt levels reduce headroom for additional borrowing in a stress scenario and increase long-term interest cost exposure.

findings.headline: HRA financing costs rise from 28.32% to 33.33% of revenue over the decade, representing an escalating burden on social housing finance
findings.detail: The Housing Revenue Account's ratio of financing costs to net revenue stream increases steadily from 28.32% in 2026/27, peaking at 33.33% in 2034/35. This is driven by £475.2m of planned HRA capital investment and rising depreciation charges. The upward trend leaves little flexibility for additional HRA expenditure or investment.
findings.matters: HRA financing cost ratios above 30% indicate stress in the housing finance model and significantly constrain discretionary HRA spending and reserves.

findings.headline: £44.373m of capital funding deferred through reserve drawdown will require future borrowing
findings.detail: The council's Capital Financing Requirement is £904.315m but actual external borrowing is £729.074m, leaving £44.373m (adjusted for PFI) unfunded from borrowing. The council has intentionally used cash reserves for capital expenditure to defer borrowing. The document explicitly notes this creates a future obligation: 'It must be borne in mind however that this difference will need to be financed in the future and, when the timing is considered right, further borrowing will be undertaken.'
findings.matters: Deferring borrowing by drawing reserves only works if reserves are adequate. This creates a forward-looking funding requirement that the council will eventually need to finance, likely at whatever rates prevail at that future time. Lenders need to understand whether reserve balances are sufficient to sustain this strategy.
findings.figures: £44.373m unborrowed liability; CFR £904.315m vs actual borrowing £729.074m
findings.quote: It must be borne in mind however that this difference will need to be financed in the future and, when the timing is considered right, further borrowing will be undertaken.

findings.headline: £78.88m of loans mature and require refinancing within 24 months at current higher rates
findings.detail: At 31 March 2025, £39.165m of loans mature within one year (averaging 5.37%) and £39.715m within 1-2 years (averaging 5.45%). These maturities will need to be refinanced at current market rates. The council's own disclosure shows current PWLB rates at 5.42-5.91%, well above the 4-4.5% average of existing debt, creating upward pressure on debt service costs.
findings.matters: Significant debt maturity concentrated in the near term creates refinancing risk. The council will be forced to roll over nearly £40m per year into a higher interest rate environment, incrementally increasing debt service costs at a time of tight budget margins.
findings.figures: £39.165m due within 1 year (5.37% rate); £39.715m in 1-2 years (5.45% rate); PWLB 10-year rates at 5.42%

findings.headline: Total annual interest charges up 35.6% to £27.097m, driven by higher rates and additional borrowing
findings.detail: Debt service costs increased from £19.991m in 2023/24 to £27.097m in 2024/25. The council took new borrowing averaging 4.97% (new loans table) at a time of elevated rates, while base rates remain high at 4.5%. This significant increase in the cost of carrying debt will compound the pressure on the revenue budget going forward.
findings.matters: Rising debt service costs compress the council's revenue budget flexibility and demonstrate that each additional pound borrowed will cost substantially more in interest. At current rates, the affordability of future capital investment is being eroded.
findings.figures: 2024/25 £27.097m vs 2023/24 £19.991m (35.6% increase); new borrowing averaged 4.97%
findings.quote: Interest payments increased in year as a result of the authority taking on more debt.

findings.headline: Capital programme delivered only 61% of planned spend, with £68m deferred to future years
findings.detail: The capital programme budget for 2024/25 was £175.635m but actual outturn was only £107.565m, an underspend of £68.07m or 38.7%. This resulted in £31.461m of planned prudential borrowing being deferred. The document does not explain the cause of this large variance, which could signal delays in project delivery, re-prioritisation, or changes in strategy.
findings.matters: A significant divergence between planned and actual capital spending indicates delivery risk or programme volatility, which affects a lender's ability to rely on the council's capital forecasts and may signal problems in the council's project management or capital governance.
findings.figures: Budget £175.635m, actual £107.565m, underspend £68.07m (38.7%)
findings.quote: The overall underspend / slippage of £68.07m has resulted in deferred borrowing of £31.461m.

findings.headline: HRA debt interest charges nearly tripled to £8.071m from £2.783m
findings.detail: Housing Revenue Account interest payments increased from £2.783m in 2023/24 to £8.071m in 2024/25, a 190% increase in a single year. The report provides no explanation for this sharp cost shock. It suggests either significant new HRA borrowing or refinancing of existing HRA debt at substantially higher rates. Given current PWLB rates, this will likely persist or worsen.
findings.matters: A near-tripling of debt service costs on one part of the council's borrowing portfolio represents a material cost shock with direct implications for the HRA's financial sustainability and the council's consolidated budget pressure.

findings.headline: Eight audit recommendations from 2024/25 remain outstanding, indicating persistent implementation weakness
findings.detail: The council has 8 recommendations from the prior audit year (2024/25) that are still outstanding as at 25 September 2025. Combined with 10 outstanding from the current year, this suggests a systemic issue with turning audit findings into action. While many recommendations from prior years have been implemented (253 of 267 from 2022/23 to 2024/25), the tail of unimplemented findings is growing.
findings.matters: If a council repeatedly leaves audit recommendations unimplemented, it signals either that management does not regard audit findings as material, or lacks the capacity to act on them. Either is a concern.
findings.figures: 8 outstanding from 2024/25 (6 medium-risk, 2 low-risk); 10 outstanding from 2025/26 (3 high-risk); cumulative 18 outstanding
findings.quote: 2024/25: Recommendations made in previous years were also subject to ongoing monitoring: 66 recommendations were made, of those due for implementation eight remain outstanding. Of these recommendations six were of medium risk and two were of low risk.

findings.headline: Officer decision-making audit rated Marginal, indicating governance gaps in decision recording and authorization
findings.detail: The audit of officer decision-making (covering compliance with the council's Constitution and Scheme of Delegation) returned a Marginal opinion with 9 recommendations (5 medium-risk, 4 low-risk). The audit found that 'the key areas which required improvement were in respect of implementing procedures, recording and monitoring.' This suggests officers are not consistently following the council's own governance rules.
findings.matters: If officer decision-making is not properly recorded and authorized, the council lacks a clear audit trail for material decisions (including financial ones). This is a governance control that underpins accountability.
findings.figures: 9 recommendations (5 medium-risk, 4 low-risk); Marginal opinion
findings.quote: At this audit nine recommendations were made (five medium risks and four low risks), with the resultant audit opinion of 'Marginal'. The key areas which required improvement were in respect of implementing procedures, recording and monitoring.

findings.headline: Three high-risk audit recommendations remain unimplemented, with eight of ten outstanding recommendations from a single flawed audit
findings.detail: As at 25 September 2025, the council had 10 outstanding recommendations due for implementation in the current year (2025/26), of which 3 are rated high-risk. The report notes that 8 of these 10 outstanding came from the NHS Health Checks audit (issued May 2025), which itself received an Unsatisfactory opinion. This concentration suggests either implementation difficulty or resource constraints.
findings.matters: High-risk audit findings that remain unimplemented indicate either that the council cannot fix the problem or is not prioritizing it. When high-risk items persist unimplemented for months, lenders should ask why.
findings.figures: 10 outstanding recommendations in 2025/26 (3 high-risk, 5 medium, 2 low); 8 of the 10 from NHS Health Checks audit
findings.quote: Of those due for implementation 10 were outstanding, of which three were of high risk, five were of medium risk and two were of low risk. Of the 10 recommendations eight were in respect of the NHS Health Check issued in May 2025.

findings.headline: Fraud losses totalled £2.7 million in 2024/25.
findings.detail: The Corporate Fraud Team identified and recovered £2.7 million in fraud across multiple categories including housing tenancy fraud, council tax fraud, blue badge fraud, and insurance fraud. The council will face a new criminal offence of failure to prevent fraud coming into force from September 2025.
findings.matters: Fraud detection at this scale indicates either significant fraud exposure or weaknesses in preventive controls. The incoming legislative requirement to prevent fraud will create new compliance and financial risks if controls are not strengthened.
findings.figures: £2.7m in fraud detected for the year 1 April 2024 to 31 March 2025
findings.quote: The Committee was advised that the value of fraud for the year overall amounted to £2.7m.

findings.headline: Council in Exceptional Financial Support with a structural deficit difficult to address.
findings.detail: The council has received Exceptional Financial Support (EFS) from central government for 2023-24 and 2024-25, with a further request for 2025-26. An independent CIPFA review concluded the council has a structural deficit that is difficult to address, arising from national funding reductions and increasing demand for social care. The review found the council well-governed but structurally unable to balance finances without ongoing central support.
findings.matters: Exceptional Financial Support signals the council cannot meet spending obligations from its own resources. A structural deficit that persists across multiple years and requires repeated central government support indicates fundamental financial instability, which is a material credit risk for lenders.
findings.figures: EFS requested for 2023-24, 2024-25, and 2025-26; structural deficit identified as difficult to address
findings.quote: Due to national funding reductions and increasing demand for services such as social care and the impact of inflation, the scale of the challenges had resulted in the council needing to apply for Exceptional Financial Support (EFS) from central government for the 2023-24 and 2024-25 financial years. Further support had also been requested in 2025-26.

findings.headline: 2024/25 audit fees remain unconfirmed and specialist costs will increase, putting strain on finance teams already identified as a risk.
findings.detail: The 2024/25 audit fee structure has multiple line items marked 'TBC' (to be confirmed). In 2023/24, total audit fees were £241,445 including £34,822 in additional costs for valuation and IT specialists. The report explicitly notes 'officer capacity and the potential strain to the finance and related teams' as risks in delivering the rebuilding work.
findings.matters: Rising audit costs combined with acknowledged resource constraints in the finance function indicate the council will face both financial and operational pressure during the assurance rebuild.
findings.figures: 2023/24 total fees £241,445; specialist costs £8,025 (valuation) plus £19,225 (IT). 2024/25 baseline scale fee £481,391 with additional costs TBC.
findings.quote: We are still expecting further guidance on the work required to follow this approach, so there are risks and challenges to overcome, not just in terms of volume of work required, auditor capacity, but also officer capacity and the potential strain to the finance and related teams.

findings.headline: Auditors chose a multi-year 'historic testing approach' rather than the faster 'proof in total' method, indicating substantial issues with historical financial records.
findings.detail: Rather than using the proof in total approach (which could complete in one year), Mazars selected the historic testing approach requiring full substantive testing of prior-period transactions over multiple years. The auditors state this decision 'was not taken lightly' and cite timeline constraints and the need to support the entire local government system.
findings.matters: Choosing the more protracted rebuilding method suggests the extent of control weaknesses and financial record issues is too significant for a quicker recovery path.
findings.figures: Historic testing approach begins 2025/26 and continues through at least 2028/29.
findings.quote: Taking into account relevant factors, we believe the only option is the historic testing approach and for 2024/25 we intend to issue a disclaimed audit report. This decision was not taken lightly.

findings.headline: The council has received disclaimed audit opinions since 2020/21 with no expectation of a clean opinion before 2028/29.
findings.detail: Stoke-on-Trent's audit reports shifted from unmodified opinions (2018/19, 2019/20) to disclaimed opinions from 2020/21 onwards. The auditors' timeline shows disclaimed opinions continuing through 2026/27, with only a possibility of qualified opinions in 2027/28 and 2028/29. This represents four consecutive years without proper audit assurance.
findings.matters: Disclaimed audit opinions mean the council's financial statements have not been audited and their integrity cannot be assured, a fundamental credibility issue for any lender assessing the council's financial position.
findings.figures: Disclaimed opinions: 2020/21, 2021/22, 2022/23, 2023/24. Auditors expect disclaimed opinions through 2026/27, qualified opinions at earliest in 2027/28.
findings.quote: Year: 2020/21 2021/22 2022/23 2023/24 ... Form of audit report: Disclaimed Disclaimed Disclaimed Disclaimed

findings.headline: Council identifies loss of stakeholder confidence as material risk from persistent audit disclaimers
findings.detail: The paper explicitly lists 'Loss of stakeholder confidence and increased political scrutiny' as a key risk, indicating the council recognizes that five years of disclaimed opinions has damaged or is at risk of damaging confidence in financial management.
findings.matters: Loss of stakeholder confidence is a governance risk that affects the council's ability to operate effectively, access capital, and maintain relationships with partners and lenders.
findings.figures: Risk identified in section 4.3
findings.quote: Risk: Loss of stakeholder confidence and increased political scrutiny.

findings.headline: Finance team will face sustained increased audit demands over 3–4 years
findings.detail: The council explicitly acknowledges that historic testing will require substantial work from council officers and identifies key risk of 'Significant sustained pressure on finance capacity causing delays to routine statutory deadlines.' The paper notes 'Short-term increased workload will impact the finance and service staff.'
findings.matters: Stretched finance capacity raises risk of delays in financial close, reporting errors, or inability to respond to audit queries efficiently, compounding the audit weakness.
findings.figures: 3–4 years of increased demands
findings.quote: The Council must prepare for increased audit demands over the next 3–4 years.

findings.headline: 2024/25 audit fee unconfirmed but certain to exceed 2023/24 fee of £241,445
findings.detail: The 2023/24 audit fee was £241,445. The 2024/25 fee remains unconfirmed and will be determined by the scope of historic testing and additional audit procedures, creating budgetary uncertainty.
findings.matters: Rising audit fees add budget pressure to an already-stressed finance function, and the open-ended nature of the fee creates planning uncertainty.
findings.figures: 2023/24 fee: £241,445; 2024/25 fee unconfirmed
findings.quote: The 2023/24 audit fee totalled £241,445. The 2024/25 fee is yet to be confirmed and will depend on the scope of historic testing and additional audit procedures.

findings.headline: Audit assurance rebuild will extend through 2028/29 via multi-year historic testing programme
findings.detail: Auditors have adopted historic testing—sampling and testing prior-year transactions in depth—as the rebuild method. This programme is expected to run from 2025/26 through 2028/29, meaning the council will remain unable to provide clean financial statements for four more years.
findings.matters: The extended timeline prolongs uncertainty about financial reporting accuracy, delaying normal audit conclusions for another four years and keeping the council in a form of financial reporting limbo.
findings.quote: That programme involves a detailed examination of prior-year transactions and records and is expected to run across several years (estimated 2025/26 to 2028/29).

findings.headline: Five consecutive disclaimed audit opinions from 2020/21 through 2024/25
findings.detail: Stoke-on-Trent has received disclaimed audit opinions for five consecutive years and the auditors intend to issue the same for 2024/25. Disclaimed opinions mean the auditors cannot verify the totals of the council's accounts end-to-end, indicating material weakness in financial reporting assurance.
findings.matters: A borrower unable to produce verified accounts across five consecutive years presents elevated financial reporting risk, making due diligence and lending decisions difficult.
findings.figures: 2020/21 to 2023/24 = four disclaimed opinions; 2024/25 = intended disclaimer
findings.quote: Stoke-on-Trent City Council received disclaimed opinions for the years 2020/21 to 2023/24. The auditors have indicated they are likely to issue a disclaimer for 2024/25 as well
